svg.title: The recorded call sequence of a successful write and a failed one
svg.desc: Two recorded traces side by side, drawn on the same step positions so the first four calls line up exactly. On the left, the success path: acquire a connection from the write pool, BEGIN, execute the statement, insert the audit row on that same connection, and COMMIT. A green bracket runs from BEGIN down past COMMIT, marking the audit insert as being inside the transaction, and the result reads status committed with two rows affected and audit identifier seventeen. A quiet line partway down the left panel says no second acquire is needed there, because the audit row is already inside. On the right, the failure path: the same first three calls, then ROLLBACK, then a dashed rule at exactly that height marking everything below it as being after the rollback and on a new connection, then a second acquire from the write pool and a second audit insert recording success as false. The red bracket on the right closes at the rollback, so the last two steps sit outside it, because the transaction that would have carried the audit row no longer exists. That result reads status failed with zero rows affected and the message PostgreSQL returned. Notes add that had the audit insert raised on the left the write above it would have rolled back with it, and that the second acquire on the right must come from the write pool, since taking it from the read pool is why the first edition of the project recorded not one failure.
svg.text: Success is one transaction. Failure is a transaction that is gone, plus a second, separate write.
The change and the record of it commit together.
no second acquire: the audit row is already inside
Had the audit insert raised, the DELETE above it would
have rolled back with it. Nothing changes unlogged.
Failure · a transaction that is gone
so the audit row has to be a second, separate write.
after the rollback, on a new connection
Step 5 must come from the write pool. Pointing it at the read
pool is why the first edition recorded not one failure.
The entries you most want in an audit log are the failures, and they are the ones a shared connection accessor quietly loses.
